newsitem.title: USA: Rates seen falling as economy cools, some analysts now say.
newsitem.headline: Rates seen falling as economy cools, some analysts now say.

text.p: While many economists have been predicting interest rates will rise later this year, a few actually expect rates to remain steady or fall over the next 12 months.
"You can expect that minority view to become a majority view in the weeks and months ahead," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc.
"This is a very different type of economic cycle," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.

"Inflation is subdued and set to remain subdued, and economic growth is likely to slow to a steadier pace over the next six to 12 months. Against that background, there is no need for the Fed to tighten."

That view stands in marked contrast to those that had the market predicting a 0.25 percentage point increase in short term rates earlier this week, as the Federal Reserve debated the state of the economy and the need for a change in interest rates.

Low unemployment, rising wages and increasing retail sales all pointed to an accelerating economy, factors that would be expected to favour an increase in interest rates to prevent inflation, said Robert Forrestal, former Atlanta Fed president and now a partner at law firm Smith Gambrell and Russell.
The Federal Reserve decided on Tuesday to hold short-term rates steady.
"We think the Federal Reserve is basically on vacation for at least until the middle of winter," said Vincent Malanga, an economist at LaSalle Economics in New York.

Economists note that long-term rates in the bond market already have risen to about 6.90 percent from 6.03 percent in January, when the Fed last changed short-term rates, cutting them by a quarter point in a bid to spur economic growth.
The Fed controls two key short-term rates but long-term bond rates fluctuate according to market forces.

In addition, bank loan growth has slowed, consumer debt has swollen to record post-war levels and the stock market's early-year rally has sputtered, all of which point to slower consumer spending in the medium to long term.

"Consumers in the first half of the year were spending money faster than it was coming in," said Bruce Steinberg, economist at Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc. "Job growth was strong, but they managed to spend a lot faster than even the income that was generated by that job growth," he said.
Consumers fuel about two-thirds of economic activity with their purchases of goods and services.

Fed policy-makers were faced with conflicting evidence on the state of the economy when they met on Tuesday. By opting not to raise rates, the Fed was betting that economic growth will slow enough on its own to head off the risk of higher inflation down the road, analysts said.

"Greenspan started the second half of the year with a firm view that the economy was going to slow down early enough and fast enough to to head off any inflationary pressures before they really began building," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
"Now in September, with the August data and particularly the retail sales and the trade numbers, he's got some modest amount of hope that his forecast will come true," he added.
Reports out Thursday also pointed to a slowing economy. Orders for costly manufactured goods tumbled in August while new applications for jobless pay surged last week, the government reported.

Meanwhile, recent increases in wages will not necessarily feed a pickup in inflation, analysts said, noting companies faced with stiff global competition are hesitant to raise prices, even if labour costs are rising.
"The labour market is tight and wage rates are rising, but it hasn't produced any inflation yet," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
If the forecasts for slower economic growth materialise, analysts said everyone from bond investors to mortgage holders could gain.
"More often on adjusted rates, like mortage rates on equity loans and things like that ... you would see those rates going down," Levenson said.
He said he expects the Fed to cut rates in 1997.
"The first instalment, the first (quarter-point) cut in the funds rate, will come in the first quarter," he said.

The federal funds rate, which banks charge each other for overnight loans, is 5.25 percent, and the discount rate, which the Fed charges banks for loans, is 5 percent. The Fed has held the rates steady since cutting each by a quarter point on Jan. 31.
